content:
In the past few days, two reports have proposed different ways Apple could earn more profit by increasing services revenue.

In my view, Apple should definitely do the former, but should not do the latter — and it seems Phil Schiller appears to very much agree with this take...

First, let me summarise the content of these two reports.

Home security and monitoring services

On Friday, *Bloomberg* revealed that Apple may be planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, designed to work with some of the new home hardware products we have been anticipating.

Squeezing more profit from the App Store

A second report published by the same source on Sunday indicates that Apple is exploring how it can squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple should not take the latter approach

I believe the second approach would be a very serious mistake.

Apple's de facto monopoly position over iPhone app sales has already come under fierce criticism from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you are forced to go through the official App Store — you have no choice at all, you must accept Apple's terms, and you have zero bargaining power.

I understand many people will say no one is forcing you to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that is not how true laissez-faire capitalism works: even in the United States, there have been antitrust laws since 1890. Once you reach a certain level of market dominance, there are corresponding restrictions to ensure you do not abuse that position.

Trying to squeeze more money out of the App Store runs completely counter to the philosophy of "skating to where the puck is going" — Schiller is reported to hold the same view, and *Bloomberg* even suggests this is one of the reasons he chose to step down from his current role.

Innovative services are the right direction

By contrast, launching innovative services that people willingly pay to use is what Apple should be doing. I can absolutely see the value of this company offering a home security monitoring service.

Back in 2024, I already said that launching its own smart home camera would be one of the smartest moves the company could make. The rumoured Apple smart doorbell is the same. Offering an optional service bundle for security products makes complete sense, for two reasons.

First, there are the various privacy reasons I mentioned previously. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a great deal of work in safeguarding the privacy of security camera footage. If I had to choose a company to trust with running AI analysis on security camera footage, I would pick Apple.

Second, Apple is of course the company best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I firmly believe there are many other areas where Apple could offer similar benefits.

For me, the key point is that Apple needs to apply the same attitude it takes toward hardware to its services — building outstanding products that people are happy and willing to pay for, rather than making money in ways that annoy customers, developers and regulators alike.

What do you think about this? Please share your views in the comments section.
